---
title: "Institutions, Coordination, and Societal Resilience"
unit_id: "unit-08"

## The Patch Leaves the Repository

A repository change begins inside a boundary that seems manageable. A maintainer
proposes it. Reviewers inspect it. Automated checks run. Someone with merge
authority accepts or rejects it. Even when the decision is difficult, the roles
can be named and the affected artifact can be identified.

Then the repository becomes infrastructure.

Other projects depend on its package. Several organizations rely on its release
service. Volunteer maintainers, commercial users, public institutions, and
people who never agreed to the project's governance are exposed to its
behavior. A change that saves the original team an hour may transfer days of
work to downstream operators. A security measure that protects one population
may deny service to another. An emergency response that is lawful in one place
may violate duties in another. A clean rollback may restore the code while
leaving financial loss, inaccessible services, damaged records, or uncorrected
public claims behind.

The engineering problem has changed. The question is no longer only whether an
authorized operator may modify an artifact. It is who can authorize effects
across institutions, whose interests count, how disagreements cross
jurisdictions, and what happens after prevention fails. Capability does not
create mandate. Technical correctness does not create legitimacy. Stopping an
incident does not by itself restore the people and institutions that absorbed
its effects.

This is where governance becomes more than a permission system. A governed AI
stack needs institutions that can turn bounded evidence into contestable
collective action, and it needs resilience mechanisms that continue after a
decision, model, provider, or control has failed. Neither layer may borrow the
other's conclusion. An institution can possess a mandate and still respond
badly. A response network can restore a service and still lack lawful authority,
representative standing, or an adequate remedy.

The central design problem is therefore not to create one global approval bit.
It is to preserve the differences among mandate, evidence, participation,
enforcement, remedy, resistance, recovery, and adaptation while allowing them
to compose under pressure.

## Capability Is Not Mandate

An AI system may be able to draft a regulation, evaluate a model, coordinate a
response, allocate compute, or disable an account. None of those capabilities
answers whether it may do so for a particular public, institution, or
jurisdiction.

Mandate is a relation, not a property of the system. It binds an actor, an
instrument, a jurisdiction, an affected population, a class of action, a time
window, and a route for challenge. The same organization can be authorized to
inspect one service and forbidden to inspect another. The same emergency power
can be valid for one incident and invalid after its expiry. The same technical
standard can be useful evidence in several countries without becoming law in
any of them.

This distinction matters because advanced systems make mandate laundering easy.
A model can produce a convincing report faster than an institution can decide
who is entitled to rely on it. A company can implement a voluntary standard and
describe the result as public legitimacy. A coordination forum can collect
signatures while leaving enforcement, withdrawal, and remedy undefined. A
technical team can inherit responsibility for a public problem simply because
it is the only group able to act quickly.

The stack should resist each substitution. Competence can qualify an actor for
a role, but cannot appoint it. Evidence can inform an authority, but cannot
create one. Standards can make expectations testable, but cannot settle who is
bound. Participation can expose disagreement, but cannot turn consultation
into consent. Speed can reduce harm, but cannot erase the need to record the
authority used and the residuals left behind.

## The Affected Public Is Part of the System

System diagrams often end at the organization that deploys the model. The
effects do not. They travel through customers, workers, contractors,
communities, public services, supply chains, information environments, and
institutions with unequal capacity to respond.

An affected-party map is therefore not a public-relations appendix. It is part
of the control surface. It should name direct users, non-user subjects,
downstream dependents, operators, reviewers, maintainers, populations exposed
to externalities, institutions expected to provide remedy, and groups likely to
bear the cost of a failure or a safeguard. It should also record uncertainty:
unknown dependents and unrepresented populations do not disappear because the
map is incomplete.

This changes the meaning of a successful intervention. Suppose a provider
blocks a malicious account. The account-level action may be correct. Yet a
complete review still asks whether copied artifacts remain elsewhere, whether
victims were notified, whether false records were corrected, whether a public
service stayed available, whether investigators preserved evidence lawfully,
and whether the attacker moved to another provider. The provider owns only part
of the path.

The same rule applies to benefits. A deployment can improve aggregate
throughput while concentrating decision power, reducing meaningful exit, or
making a weaker institution dependent on a stronger one. Average performance
does not identify who gained agency, who lost it, or who can contest the new
arrangement. Those are separate observations.

## Participation Is Not Representation

Counting participants is attractive because it produces a clean number. A
large consultation, a public comment period, a standards meeting, or a
multi-stakeholder panel can demonstrate that a process opened a door. The count
cannot establish who walked through it, who could not, whose input changed the
decision, or whether the participants had standing to represent anyone beyond
themselves.

Representation requires a theory of constituency and accountability. Who
selected the representative? What information did that person receive? Could
the represented group replace them? Were dissenting positions preserved? Did
language, time, expertise, disability, money, or fear of retaliation determine
who could participate? Was the decision already fixed before participation
began?

This does not mean every technical change requires a plebiscite. It means the
form of participation should match the decision and its effects. A maintainer
may decide an internal refactor. A change that alters contractual obligations
needs the parties named by those contracts. A cross-border public deployment
may require regulators, affected institutions, technical evaluators, civil
society, and harmed-party routes with different kinds of standing. Expertise,
democratic authority, ownership, operational responsibility, and lived exposure
are not interchangeable credentials.

A well-designed packet records the differences instead of compressing them
into a stakeholder score. It can say that a process had broad notice but weak
influence, strong technical review but poor affected-party representation, or
formal authorization but unresolved dissent. That may look less decisive. It
is more honest, and it gives later review something precise to repair.

## Jurisdiction Is a Routing Constraint

Jurisdiction is often treated as metadata attached after a system design is
complete. In a governed stack it changes the route itself.

The system needs to know which institution is acting, under which instrument,
for which population, over which action, and with which geographic or sectoral
scope. It needs conflict rules when several authorities apply, escalation when
no competent authority can be identified, expiry when emergency or temporary
powers end, and a refusal path when a requested action exceeds the recorded
mandate.

This is not a claim that law can be reduced to a policy engine. Legal meaning,
facts, precedent, institutional competence, and due process exceed a finite
schema. The record serves a narrower purpose: it prevents the runtime from
treating one valid authorization as universal. A mandate issued for one
jurisdiction should not silently authorize another. A changed instrument,
protocol, population, or territorial scope should invalidate the old receipt
until the new case is reviewed.

Cross-border coordination needs the same discipline. An international
commitment should identify parties, covered systems, entry conditions,
measurement, verification access, data-sharing limits, uncertainty,
noncompliance handling, incentives or sanctions, withdrawal, amendment,
emergency exceptions, and re-entry. A signature is evidence of a commitment,
not evidence that domestic institutions implemented it or that enforcement is
effective.

## Coordination Must Survive Partial Participation

Coordination designs frequently assume that the relevant actors will join,
report honestly, interpret terms similarly, and remain capable of carrying out
their commitments. Real systems contain nonparticipants, delayed participants,
weak institutions, strategic concealment, incompatible laws, resource
asymmetries, and actors who benefit from the others' restraint.

The architecture should model those states before an emergency. For each
commitment, it should ask what can be observed, who verifies it, how shared
dependencies are disclosed, how disagreement is recorded, what happens when a
party cannot perform, and which actions remain possible when a party refuses.
The strongest actor should not become the default global authority merely
because it has the fastest telemetry or the largest response team.

This is why commitment and enforcement must remain separate. A beautifully
specified treaty, policy, or protocol can coexist with weak inspection,
selective enforcement, inaccessible remedy, or no capacity to act. Conversely,
an institution may have strong enforcement capacity but no legitimate mandate
for the proposed action. A coordination packet should make both failures
visible.

It should also preserve strategic feedback. If complying actors incur high
cost while noncomplying actors capture the benefit, the arrangement may
collapse. If verification requires data that weaker parties cannot collect,
formal equality can produce practical exclusion. If emergency exceptions are
easy to invoke and hard to retire, temporary coordination can become permanent
centralization. These are system dynamics, not footnotes.

## Resilience Has Four Different Verbs

Prevention is necessary, but prevention-only governance is brittle. Some attacks
will pass. Some models will be misused. Some safeguards will fail. Some harms
will come from ordinary errors, institutional conflict, cascading dependencies,
or slow shifts that no single incident detector recognizes.

Societal resilience begins by separating four capacities.

**Resist** means reducing the probability or reach of a harmful event before it
takes hold. Authentication, access control, hardened services, careful release,
training, redundancy, public education, and defensive tools can all contribute.
Resistance is not absolute prevention; it is measured against a threat and an
exposed population.

**Absorb** means continuing essential functions while the event is active.
Fallback communication, service degradation plans, manual procedures,
alternative providers, trusted intermediaries, and protected reserves can keep
one failure from becoming total institutional collapse. Absorption can impose
unequal burdens, so continuity metrics need affected-party measures as well as
uptime.

**Recover** means restoring services, rights, records, resources, and agency
after containment. Re-enabling an account or reverting code may be part of
recovery, but harmed-party remedy, correction, compensation, support, and
institutional repair may continue long afterward. A provider's terminal state
is not necessarily the victim's terminal state.

**Adapt** means changing the system in response to what was learned without
creating a new unreviewed hazard. Playbooks, training, technical controls,
coordination agreements, and laws may all change. Adaptation should name the
evidence, affected parties, authority, expected effect, expiry, and rollback of
the change. Updating a policy document is not evidence that field behavior
improved.

These stages overlap. Resistance continues during response. Recovery can reveal
new exposure and reopen containment. Adaptation can reduce one threat while
creating a new concentration or access failure. A resilient system therefore
does not force every incident through a neat linear pipeline. It preserves the
state of each capacity and the residuals that keep the case open.

## One Shared Service, Many Authorities

Consider a hypothetical release service used by dozens of independent software
projects. It builds packages, signs artifacts, publishes updates, and carries a
reputation for dependable automation. Some projects are volunteer-maintained.
Some are commercial. A public institution depends on one downstream package
for an essential internal service. Users in several jurisdictions receive
updates through different distributors.

The service's maintainers propose an AI-assisted change. The new controller
would identify low-risk releases, compress review steps, and publish them more
quickly. On the service's historical fixtures, the controller reduces delay and
passes the tests. Under repository-scale governance, the change looks ready.

The institutional view asks different questions. Who authorized the service to
classify risk for downstream projects? Did those projects delegate publication
authority or only build execution? Which users are affected by a false low-risk
classification? Does a public institution have duties that prevent automated
updates without its own review? Can a volunteer project realistically inspect
the evidence packet? Which jurisdiction governs a disputed signature or an
incorrectly withdrawn release? Who may pause the shared service, and who can
continue operating if it is paused?

Suppose the controller publishes a flawed dependency. The release service
detects the anomaly and stops further publication. That is resistance arriving
late and containment arriving early. It is useful, but the system has not
recovered.

Some downstream projects already incorporated the package. One distributor
cached it. The public institution disables an affected service while it
investigates. A volunteer maintainer cannot respond immediately. Users receive
conflicting notices because each organization knows only part of the incident.
No single actor has both a complete dependency map and authority over every
copy.

A governed response starts with shared incident identity rather than shared
sovereignty. Participants can refer to the same event, affected artifacts, and
time window while retaining their own duties. The release service can revoke
its signature, publish evidence, preserve logs, notify known dependents, and
offer a corrected build. Distributors can quarantine cached copies. Projects
can decide whether the corrected version satisfies their own release rules.
The public institution can follow its continuity and reporting obligations.
No actor's valid action automatically ratifies the others.

The response packet should record known and unknown affected populations,
services that must remain available, evidence-sharing rules, confidentiality
constraints, response owners, deadlines, handoffs, disputes, and residuals.
Where lawful and proportionate, participants may share minimal telemetry about
affected versions and observed failures. They should not turn incident
coordination into an unlimited data-sharing license.

Absorption might involve a stable older package, a manual workflow, or a
temporary alternative service. These routes have costs. The older package may
carry a known vulnerability. Manual operation may burden a small team.
Alternative infrastructure may be available only to wealthy participants. A
serious review records these tradeoffs instead of reporting that service was
simply “restored.”

Recovery proceeds on several clocks. The release service can restore correct
publication quickly. Downstream projects may need to rebuild and redistribute.
The public institution may need to verify records and notify affected people.
Users may need corrections or support. A project that lost trust or volunteer
capacity may not recover when the software does. Each clock needs an owner and
a criterion for closure.

Adaptation comes last only in the sense that it should be informed by the
event. The service might tighten its classifier, add a downstream approval
mode, improve dependency notification, or reduce the controller's authority.
Participants might create a mutual-aid agreement for future incidents. These
changes are new proposals, not automatic consequences of the postmortem. They
need their own evidence, mandate, burden review, and rollback path.

The example reveals why one global score would be misleading. The release
service can improve mean recovery time while weaker projects recover more
slowly. The corrected package can be technically sound while notices remain
inaccessible. Most participants can approve a new coordination agreement while
the most exposed population lacks representation. The architecture needs a
joint picture without erasing these differences.

## Remedy Must Reach the Harmed Party

Remedy is often attached to governance as an appeals address. For a complex AI
system, it is an end-to-end path.

A person or institution must be able to discover that a decision or incident
affected them, identify the responsible route, preserve relevant evidence,
challenge facts or authority, receive a timely response, obtain correction or
other relief where appropriate, and escalate when the first institution cannot
act. The route should survive vendor changes, model replacement, organizational
restructuring, and cross-border handoffs.

This does not imply that every bad outcome has one liable actor or one complete
repair. Adaptive systems and shared infrastructure can create uncertain,
distributed causation. The answer is not to erase responsibility because it is
hard to allocate. The system can record contribution hypotheses, confidence,
disputes, evidence custody, provisional measures, and unresolved residuals
while the competent institutions adjudicate the case.

Remedy is also distinct from resilience metrics. Rapid containment does not
show that an injured party was restored. High service availability does not
show that burdens were equitable. Compensation does not establish that the
system is now safe. Each result answers a different question.

## Concentration and Gradual Loss of Human Influence

Not every institutional failure arrives as an incident. AI systems may produce
gradual shifts in who can understand, contest, finance, or perform important
work. Each local adoption can appear voluntary and useful while the combined
system becomes hard to exit.

A shared evaluator may become the only practical route to market. A handful of
providers may control compute, identity, model access, or incident telemetry.
Organizations may retain formal approval while losing the expertise and time
needed to disagree. Public institutions may depend on private systems they
cannot inspect. Workers and communities may be consulted after the operational
alternatives have disappeared.

This is gradual disempowerment as a systems problem: human influence can erode
without one agent seizing power and without one decision crossing a dramatic
threshold. The relevant signals include concentration, switching cost,
dependency depth, review capacity, skill retention, option diversity,
meaningful appeal, and the ability of affected groups to form and finance
alternatives.

The response cannot be a blanket ban on scale or specialization. Shared
infrastructure can make strong security, evidence, and recovery available to
small institutions. The design goal is to keep shared capability from becoming
unreviewable authority. Interoperability, portable records, independent
evaluation, federated response capacity, fork and exit paths, local competence,
and explicit sunset review can preserve alternatives. None guarantees a fair
distribution of power, but each makes loss of agency more observable and
contestable.

## Failure Cases

**Legitimacy laundering.** A company cites technical conformance, a consultation,
or an international principle as if it were public authorization. The repair is
to name the actual mandate, jurisdiction, instrument, affected population, and
challenge route. If those fields cannot be supplied, the action should not be
described as institutionally authorized.

**Participation without influence.** A process collects comments after the key
decision is fixed, counts attendees instead of tracing representation, or
invites groups without giving them the information and time needed to respond.
The participation record should show notice, access, standing, influence,
dissent, and unresolved exclusions separately.

**Forum shopping.** An actor selects the weakest jurisdiction, standard, or
review body and treats that result as sufficient everywhere. The system should
retain overlapping duties and route conflicts rather than choosing the most
convenient authorization.

**Treaty or protocol theater.** Parties sign a commitment with no measurable
obligations, verification access, noncompliance process, capacity plan, or
domestic implementation. The signature belongs in the record, but the
enforcement and outcome states remain open.

**Emergency ratchet.** A temporary power or centralized response is activated
quickly and never meaningfully expires. Every emergency route needs scope,
review dates, sunset conditions, retained rights, and an effect-complete path
back to ordinary governance.

**Coordination capture.** The organization with the most data, compute, or
staff defines the incident, controls the evidence, and sets closure criteria.
Shared incident identity should not entail shared control. Independent custody,
dispute routes, and separately owned recovery measures are necessary.

**Prevention-only success.** A dashboard reports blocked attempts while omitting
successful bypasses, downstream displacement, service disruption, harmed-party
recovery, and attacker adaptation. Denominators, null outcomes, and residuals
must remain visible.

**Provider-terminal recovery.** A platform closes the case after disabling an
account or restoring a service even though copied artifacts, false records,
financial losses, or affected-party needs remain. Closure needs an explicit
scope. One actor can finish its action without declaring the incident socially
resolved.

**Resilience as permission to take avoidable risk.** Operators point to backups,
insurance, or recovery plans to justify a hazardous deployment. Recovery
capacity does not lower the probability of harm unless evidence shows a causal
effect, and it does not waive duties to prevent avoidable harm.

**Permanent quarantine.** A system avoids visible recurrence by indefinitely
withholding a service, account, or capability. Containment can be necessary,
but it is not recovery when essential function, rights, or appeal never return.

**Adaptation theater.** A policy, playbook, or model card is updated after an
incident, yet behavior, resources, authority, and field performance remain
unchanged. Adaptation claims need observed implementation and outcome measures.

**Aggregate resilience.** Average recovery improves while vulnerable
populations experience longer outages, greater surveillance, inaccessible
remedy, or higher switching costs. Population identity and distributional
measures must survive aggregation.

**Slow institutional dependence.** Every individual adoption is approved, but
review skills, alternative providers, and local operating capacity decay. A
periodic legitimacy and resilience review should examine option loss, not just
incident counts.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest alternative is not no governance. It is a compact arrangement:
ordinary law and contracts, a competent regulator or accountable governing
body, established incident-response practice, clear organizational ownership,
and interoperable technical standards. Many systems should use exactly that
instead of inventing a new institutional protocol.

The stack earns its additional machinery only when several conditions occur
together: effects cross authorities, evidence changes quickly, responsibility
is distributed, important dependencies are shared, harms can outlive the
provider's response, and no one institution can observe or repair the whole
path. Even then, the new records should connect existing institutions rather
than pretend to replace them.

A fair comparison would hold the incident, participants, powers, resources,
privacy constraints, and recovery goals constant. It would compare coordination
delay, missed handoffs, wrongful action, participant burden, affected-party
recovery, institutional capture, residual closure, and total cost. If ordinary
arrangements perform as well with less complexity, they should be preferred.

## What the Current Work Can Establish

The live technical chapters provide two bounded formal reviews. They establish
properties of authored finite records, not real institutional legitimacy or
population resilience.

`AsiStackProofs.InstitutionalLegitimacyReview` contains 32 theorem declarations
over an eight-transition review. The local validation surface checks 45
single-axis admission mutations and requires an exact repair or refusal for
each. Within that model, a mandate tied to one jurisdiction cannot authorize a
different jurisdiction, and changes to the jurisdiction, instrument,
population, or protocol invalidate the associated receipt. Two
non-identifiability results show that identical participation signals can
coexist with different representation states, and identical commitment signals
can coexist with different enforcement states.

Those are useful negative results. They block a record system from claiming
that participant counts determine representative standing or that commitment
signals determine effective enforcement. They do not establish lawful
authority, representativeness, enforcement efficacy, remedy, public legitimacy,
geopolitical stability, or safety.

`AsiStackProofs.SocietalResilienceReview` also contributes 32 theorem
declarations over an eight-transition finite review. It keeps incident and
population identity, cross-organization coordination, resistance, absorption,
recovery, remedy, adaptation, and non-authority distinct. Its local review
checks exact dispositions for the chapter's bounded mutation set and includes
non-identifiability results that prevent response activity or speed from
determining affected-population recovery and remedy.

Again, the value is in what the model refuses to compress. A complete response
record does not prove that people recovered. A fast response does not establish
lawful or equitable remedy. A resilience packet does not authorize deployment,
raise a claim's support state, or prove acceptable residual harm.

This Human Reader synthesis does not combine the two finite reviews into a
stronger theorem. The institutional chapter owns mandate, jurisdiction,
participation, enforcement, and legitimacy. The resilience chapter owns the
domain-specific resist, absorb, recover, and adapt network. Their composition is
a design argument whose real-world performance remains untested here.

The external sources mapped by the live chapters provide legal, standards,
incident-response, AI-risk, and international-coordination comparators. They
support the vocabulary and reveal neighboring practices. They do not prove that
this architecture is lawful, effective, representative, equitable, or state of
the art in deployment.

## From a Minimum Packet to a Mature Governance Fabric

The minimum viable implementation is a shared packet, not a new world
government. For one cross-organizational service, record the decision or
incident identity, participating institutions, claimed mandates, jurisdictions,
affected populations, relevant instruments, evidence references, data-sharing
limits, response roles, service dependencies, resistance and absorption state,
recovery and remedy owners, disputes, expiry, and residuals. Give each actor a
way to sign, reject, narrow, or annotate its portion without endorsing the
whole.

Exercise the packet in a tabletop scenario before attaching it to live
authority. Introduce conflicting jurisdictions, missing participants, a weak
institution, delayed evidence, an inaccessible remedy route, a provider
outage, a false recovery signal, and an emergency power that should expire.
Measure whether the participants identify the conflict, route the decision,
preserve evidence, maintain essential function, reach affected parties, and
retire temporary authority. A successful tabletop demonstrates process behavior
under the chosen scenario, not societal safety.

A stronger implementation connects the packet to real dependency inventories,
incident systems, legal and policy registries, public notices, independent
evidence custody, service-level monitoring, appeal channels, and harmed-party
support. Interfaces should expose only the information required for the role;
coordination is not a license for ambient surveillance. Receipts should state
what each actor observed and did, not imply agreement on facts beyond its
competence.

The mature system is a federated governance fabric. Institutions retain their
mandates and legal forms while interoperating through typed commitments,
incident identities, evidence references, dispute routes, and recovery
contracts. Affected publics can discover decisions, understand which authority
acted, contest relevant facts or mandates, and follow remedy across handoffs.
Independent evaluators can challenge technical claims. Weaker institutions can
draw on shared defensive capacity without surrendering all local authority.
Concentration, option loss, and review-capacity decline are monitored as slow
hazards alongside acute incidents.

Maturity also changes the optimization target. The system does not maximize
agreement or speed. It seeks sufficient coordination while preserving lawful
disagreement, meaningful participation, rights, local competence, and recovery.
It measures prevented and realized harm, continuity, remedy, adaptation,
distributional burden, institutional capacity, privacy cost, response delay,
and total governance work. No single metric controls admission.

## The Strongest Objection

Institutional machinery can become the problem it claims to solve. Large
organizations can dominate standards and evidence. Incumbents can turn
compliance cost into a barrier to entry. Committees can diffuse responsibility
until no one owns the outcome. Cross-border processes can move too slowly for a
fast incident. Rich participants can satisfy record requirements that weaker
ones cannot. A technically elaborate packet can create an aura of legitimacy
without changing power.

This objection has teeth because more structure is not automatically more
accountability. The answer must be architectural and empirical. The minimum
packet should remain small. Authority, evidence, and remedy should have named
owners. Decision deadlines and emergency paths should exist, but emergency
powers should expire. Participation should record influence and exclusion, not
just attendance. Shared infrastructure should provide capacity to weaker
institutions without requiring them to accept the strongest actor's entire
policy. Independent challenge, transparent residuals, fork and exit paths, and
periodic sunset review should constrain institutional accumulation.

Even these measures may fail. Capture, delay, and unequal capacity are not bugs
that a schema can eliminate. The proposal is justified only if tested
arrangements improve real coordination and recovery without imposing greater
domination, surveillance, exclusion, or delay than their alternatives.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

The architecture should become smaller if leaner institutions preserve
standing, jurisdiction, challenge, coordination, response, remedy, and recovery
with lower capture risk and burden. It should change if affected parties cannot
use its routes, if institutions routinely treat packet completion as
legitimacy, if privacy-preserving coordination cannot provide adequate incident
visibility, or if emergency response remains too slow.

It should be rejected in a domain if the machinery systematically centralizes
authority, excludes weaker participants, delays necessary action, or produces
no measurable improvement in harmed-party outcomes. Evidence should include
natural incidents and exercises, complete attempt denominators, distributional
outcomes, independent evaluation, cross-institution reproduction, and transfer
across jurisdictions and threat classes. A successful fixture or formal record
review is not enough.

## What This Establishes

Governance at institutional scale is not one larger permission system. It is a
composition of mandates, jurisdictions, evidence, participation, enforcement,
remedy, and resilience capacities that must remain distinct even while they
coordinate.

The practical rule is simple to state and hard to implement: no actor should
gain public authority from technical capability, and no provider should declare
societal recovery from the completion of its own response. Shared records can
make those substitutions harder. Finite proofs can protect exact boundaries in
the record logic. Neither supplies legitimacy or resilience by itself.

Part I has now moved from the system boundary to the public institutions around
it. Part II turns inward again. Its first question is how a capability can
change behind these boundaries without inheriting readiness, authority, or
support from the component it replaces.
